# tsuzuri

A personal blog: a portrait and bio on the home page, and posts underneath.
Each post can carry more than one translation, and a reader is served
whichever translation best matches the locales their browser sends.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
```

## Commands

| Command                | What it does                                              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run dev`           | Serves the site locally with hot reload.                   |
| `npm run build`         | Builds the production bundle.                              |
| `npm run start`         | Serves a build produced by `npm run build`.                |
| `npm run format`        | Rewrites the project in place to its house style.          |
| `npm run format:check`  | Reports formatting drift without rewriting anything.       |
| `npm run lint`          | Lints the whole project; also checks formatting.           |
| `npm run typecheck`     | Type-checks the project. The test runner compiles without checking types, so this is the only thing that does. |
| `npm test`              | Runs the unit test suite.                                  |
| `npm run test:e2e`      | Runs the end-to-end suite. Builds the app and serves it first, so it needs a browser — `npx playwright install chromium` once per machine. |

## Layout

- `app/(site)/` — the reader-facing route group: the home page, the post
  detail page, and the small data module they both read from.
- `shared/` — code shared by more than one part of the app, independent of any
  one route. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is the locale-fallback logic a
  post detail page calls into; `shared/blog-post-slug.ts` is the slug shape
  every post's `slug` is validated against.
- `shared/*.spec.ts` — unit tests, colocated with the code they cover.
- `e2e/` — end-to-end specs, kept apart from the unit tests above because they
  exercise the whole running app rather than one module in isolation.
- `docs/` — operational notes that do not belong in code comments, such as
  [deployment](docs/deployment.md).
- `.github/workflows/` — the checks that run on every pull request.

## Contributing

Changes go through a pull request rather than landing straight on `main`.
Before writing code, sketch the plan and get it approved — this catches a
misunderstood requirement while it is still cheap to redirect, rather than
after the diff exists. A pull request is reviewed by someone other than the
person who wrote it, and merges only once that review is clean and the checks
above pass.

I read `shared/resolve-translation.ts` and its call site. Here's what the tests should actually verify, organized by the four exported functions:

**`normalizeLocale`**
- Case-insensitivity: `"EN-US"`, `"en-us"`, `"en-US"` all produce the same value.
- Trims incidental whitespace.

**`findExactMatch`**
- Matches only an identical (normalized) locale tag — `"en-US"` matches a translation tagged `"en-US"`, but *not* one tagged `"en"` or `"en-GB"` (that's the case the doc comment explicitly calls out as `findLanguageMatch`'s job, not this one's).
- Returns `null` when `post.translations` is empty or has no match.

**`findLanguageMatch`**
- Region is ignored: request `"ja-JP"` reaches a translation tagged `"ja"`, and the reverse — request `"ja"` reaches a translation tagged `"ja-JP"` — since the comment specifically claims both directions.
- Doesn't false-match a different language sharing no subtag (e.g. `"en"` vs `"es"`).

**`resolveTranslation`** — this is the one with real behavior to lock down, per its documented resolution order:
1. Exact match on the *first* accepted locale that has one — including that an exact match earlier in `acceptedLocales` wins over an exact match later in the list, and over a language-only match anywhere.
2. Falls through to language-only match when no accepted locale has an exact match, again preferring the first accepted locale that matches.
3. Falls through to `post.defaultLocale`'s translation when neither pass matches any accepted locale.
4. Returns `null` when the post has no translations at all (empty `translations` array).
5. Returns `null` when `acceptedLocales` is empty and `defaultLocale` also has no matching translation.
6. A case worth being explicit about: an exact match for a *less-preferred* accepted locale should still beat a language-only match for a *more-preferred* one, since the function does two full passes rather than resolving locale-by-locale — that's a subtle ordering choice a naive reimplementation could easily get wrong.

I'd skip testing `PostTranslation`/`Post` themselves (plain interfaces, nothing to assert) and skip re-testing `acceptedLocales()` parsing in `page.tsx` here — that header-parsing helper is route-local, not part of `shared/`, so per AGENTS.md it'd get its own colocated test rather than living in `resolve-translation.spec.ts`.

Given the project's contribution process, want me to write this up as a short plan (test file at `shared/resolve-translation.spec.ts`, cases above) before implementing?
